# Dimension values - GENERATED, DO NOT EDIT

Generated by `tools/dims.py md` from [`registry.toml`](registry.toml), which is
**authoritative for values**. Edit the registry, regenerate this.

The `machine/*.md` files stay authoritative for **reasoning** - why a number is what
it is, what it trades against, what was rejected. This table is only *what the numbers*
*are*. If a number in prose disagrees with this table, the prose is stale.

The hole drills 16 but a plug tap cannot thread the last couple of millimetres of a blind hole, so the drilled depth was never the usable figure - and reasoning from it is exactly the error that put a wrong bolt in this file twice. His challenge, 2026-10-08: the load on these four bolts is SHEAR - the screw drives vertically and the bolts run horizontally - so why would thread depth matter? It matters only through preload: a bolted joint carries shear by FRICTION between the faces, and thread is what lets you develop the clamp load that makes the friction. Run the numbers and the joint was never short: at the as-supplied 8 mm thread an M5 reached 5.7, whose aluminium shear area strips at about 11 kN against the bolt's own ~9 kN proof - THE THREAD WAS ALREADY STRONGER THAN THE BOLT, which is what the 2 x D rule of thumb exists to achieve. So the deeper tap buys preload RETENTION, not capacity: aluminium relaxes, and more turns share the load. It costs five minutes in a soft material, which is the only reason it is worth doing at all. ⚠ THE BEARING BLOCKS CANNOT HAVE THIS - their hole is 8.7 against 6 of thread, so nothing to tap into; they are steel and do not need it. |

N1-N4 cross only the web and the shim, so they can afford a thicker one, and it buys 2 mm more material under the four heads that sit beneath the lower spindle clamp. ⚠ THE PLATE THEREFORE HAS TWO COUNTERBORE DEPTHS. I had claimed all twenty could share one setting, which was tidier and wrong. |

The extra is margin against preload relaxation, not capacity. ⚠ WHAT THIS JOINT ACTUALLY NEEDS IS PRELOAD, NOT THREAD. The four bolts are in 6 mm clearance holes on M5, so 0.5 radial float per side - if the joint ever slips, that float becomes up to 1 mm of Z lost motion the controller cannot see. Friction is doing the work: at a modest 2 N.m each the four develop roughly 1.6 kN of friction capacity against a 500 N envelope. TORQUE THEM PROPERLY AND EVENLY; that matters more here than the last few millimetres of thread. Bounded at both ends like Z_BOLT_ENGAGE - too little and the thread strips, more than NUT_TAP_DEPTH and the bolt jams where the thread stops. |

The head diameter was the only variable in that sum. ⚠ THE BEAM-END BOLTS ARE NOT THIS BOLT - they stay at 17.3, see FLANGE_HEAD_D. ⚠ OPEN: whether the OTHER T-slot joints (the Y back plates, the X back plate, the casting interposer bars) also take this head or keep the 17.3. Only the front strip is FORCED by the encoder; the rest is a buy-one-bolt question and has not been asked. |
| **FLANGE_STRIP_H** | 3 mm | measured |  | TOTAL height the strip bolt’s head stands proud of the face, at its centre - 3 on the 13.8 head, his 2026-10-08. Flanged button head, hex socket in the dome, nothing above it. ✅ It is 0.8 to 1.1 ABOVE the chip’s plane - tape 1.6 plus the AS5311’s 0.3-0.6 air gap puts the chip face at 1.9-2.2 - so the head IS taller than the sensor rides. That decides nothing, because the heads are outside the lane laterally; see SENSOR_KEEPOUT_SLACK. If the puck ever has to cross a head, this is the number it has to clear. |
| **SENSOR_KEEPOUT_W** | 15 mm | part |  | 15 mm, the width the AS5311 puck needs kept clear, CENTRED OVER THE TAPE - his figure 2026-10-08, and it covers the PCB plus its mounting points rather than the chip alone. The chip itself is tiny and was never the constraint. This is the number that chose the strip bolt: see FLANGE_HEAD_D. |
| **STRIP_CHANNEL_W** | 16.2 mm | derived | STRIP_ROW_HIGH - STRIP_ROW_LOW - FLANGE_STRIP_D | 16.2 - the clear lane down the middle of the front strip, between the facing rims of the two bolt head rows. It is what the sensor puck has to fit inside. 🔴 THE BOLT ROWS ARE NOT A FREE CHOICE: STRIP_ROW_LOW and STRIP_ROW_HIGH come straight off the extrusion’s T-slots at RAIL_SLOT_INSET either side of the seam, so the ONLY way to widen this lane is a smaller flange head, which is exactly what happened on 2026-10-08. It was 12.7 at the old 17.3 head. |
| **SENSOR_KEEPOUT_SLACK** | 0.6 mm | derived | (STRIP_CHANNEL_W - SENSOR_KEEPOUT_W) / 2 | 0.6 per side, and ⚠ THAT IS THE WHOLE MARGIN ON THE ENCODER LANE. It was NEGATIVE (-1.15) at the old 17.3 head, which is to say the puck did not fit at all. 🔴 THE o9 CLEARANCE HOLES CAN EAT IT: S1-S14 are ø9 on M8 into SLIDING T-nuts, so nothing centres a bolt in its hole and ±0.5 is available. Both rows drifting inboard leaves 0.10 a side. BIAS THE STRIP BOLTS OUTBOARD WHEN TIGHTENING - it costs nothing and it is not a thing to discover after 3 m of one-shot PSA tape is down. |
| **CARRIAGE_TRAVEL** | 820 mm | measured |  | 820 mm, THE TRAVEL ON ALL THREE LONG AXES - X, Y1 and Y2 - his measurement 2026-10-09, and it closes an open item the encoder doc had been carrying with stale Mega V XL numbers. 🔴 THE METHOD IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING, because it is not obvious and a future session would otherwise re-derive it badly: put ONE bearing block at each end of the same rail, each pushed until its grease zerk touches the end plate, and measure the INSIDE distance between them. That gap is (rail span) less TWO block bodies - and the real carriage IS two butted blocks, BLOCK_BUTTED, so the gap you measure is exactly the real carriage’s travel rather than a proxy for it. The zerks are necessarily on the blocks’ OUTER ends, since otherwise a pair could not butt, so the test reproduces the real stop geometry at both ends. ✅ One figure serves all three beams: butted blocks set the carriage width on X and Y alike and every beam is BEAM_LEN, so there is one carriage length and one rail length. The stops are the X end plates meeting the back plate or a front fin. |
| **TRAVEL_RAIL_LIMITED** | 845.82 mm | derived | BEAM_LEN - BLOCK_BUTTED | 845.82 - what the travel WOULD be if the rail ends alone stopped the carriage. ✅ IT IS A CROSS-CHECK, NOT THE FIGURE TO USE: CARRIAGE_TRAVEL is measured at 820 and that is what sizes the tape. The two agree to 25.82, which is TRAVEL_LOST_TO_STOPS - the end plates standing inboard of the rail ends plus the zerks’ own protrusion. ⚠ It takes BEAM_LEN as a stand-in for rail length; the rails are 17 x M5 at 60 pitch, so about a metre, not exactly it. Close enough to confirm the measurement is the right size and nowhere near good enough to replace it. |
| **TRAVEL_LOST_TO_STOPS** | 25.82 mm | derived | TRAVEL_RAIL_LIMITED - CARRIAGE_TRAVEL | 25.82 - what the end plates take off the rail-limited travel, about 13 a side. Recorded because it is the number that moves if a stop face ever changes: the fin gets thicker, the back plate moves, or a zerk is swapped for a flush fitting. Nothing derives from it today. |
| **TAPE_STOCK** | 3000 mm | part |  | 3 m of 10 mm magnetic strip on a steel band with 3M PSA, in stock - the figure design-can-position-feedback.md has carried since 2026-08-25. 🔴 IT IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT ON THE WHOLE ENCODER LAYOUT and it is a ONE-SHOT consumable: the PSA does not survive a second lay. See TAPE_REMAINING, which is what is left after four axes. |
| **CARRIER_SECTION_L** | 220 mm | part |  | 220 mm, the printed tape carrier’s section length - his 2026-10-09, set by the Bambu P1S’s 256 x 256 bed with four laid side by side. ⚠ 220 IS NOT A ROUND NUMBER PICKED FOR TIDINESS, it is the point where two limits nearly meet: below about 206 the four sections no longer span CARRIAGE_TRAVEL at all, and much above 220 the three beams plus Z no longer come out of TAPE_STOCK. 4 x 205 was considered and rejected - it gives exactly 820, which is the travel, leaving nothing for the Hall array or the tape’s own unusable end poles. |
| **CARRIER_SECTIONS** | 4 mm | part |  | Four printed sections per beam. Four fit the bed in one run at 220 long; five would need them narrower. See CARRIER_W, which is open. |
| **TAPE_PER_BEAM** | 880 mm | derived | CARRIER_SECTION_L * CARRIER_SECTIONS | 880 mm of tape per long axis. The carrier sections butt end to end, joined by loose keys in blind sockets rather than protruding tenons - a male tenon would be swallowed at each joint and four sections would no longer reach 880. |
| **TAPE_OVERRUN_END** | 30 mm | derived | (TAPE_PER_BEAM - CARRIAGE_TRAVEL) / 2 | 30 mm of tape past each end of travel. 🔴 THE OVERRUN IS NOT SLOP, IT IS LOAD-BEARING TWICE OVER. The AS5311 datasheet gives usable stroke as the active area LESS the 2.0 mm Hall array, with the short poles at either edge of the strip excluded from the active area - so tape equal to travel is always short. And the carriage reaches its hard stops exactly when something has gone wrong, which is the worst moment for the reader to be off the end: a magnetic reader that leaves the tape and returns gives a wrong count and does not complain. At 30 a side the array never approaches an end pole, which retires the end-exclusion question rather than requiring it to be respected. |
| **TAPE_THREE_BEAMS** | 2640 mm | derived | 3 * TAPE_PER_BEAM | 2640 mm for X, Y1 and Y2. One figure times three because CARRIAGE_TRAVEL is the same on all three. |
| **TAPE_Z** | 295.91 mm | derived | Z_TRAVEL + (2 * TAPE_OVERRUN_END) | 295.91 for the Z axis, on the same overrun rule. ⚠ THE SOFTEST NUMBER IN THIS CHAIN: Z’s tape runs on the EDGE of the Z gantry plate rather than between rails, because the 1605 screw occupies the centre, and that axis has never been laid out - the encoder doc calls its reader allocation reserved rather than spent. Z_TRAVEL is firm; how much tape the edge mounting actually wants is not. |
| **TAPE_REMAINING** | 64.09 mm | derived | TAPE_STOCK - TAPE_THREE_BEAMS - TAPE_Z | 64.09 mm left of the 3 m roll after all four axes. 🔴 THAT IS THE MARGIN ON A ONE-SHOT CONSUMABLE AND IT IS THIN. It is why CARRIER_SECTION_L stops at 220: at 230 the sections come to 2760 for the three beams and the roll goes NEGATIVE once Z is counted. Any of these going up - a longer travel on one axis, a more generous overrun, a wider Z allowance - comes out of 64 mm. ⚠ Buy more tape before changing any of them, not after. |
| **FLANGE_HALF** | 8.65 mm | derived | FLANGE_HEAD_D / 2 | 8.65, the M8 equivalent of FLANGE_M5_HALF. Same reason: this is what an edge distance has to clear. 🔴 IT IS THE BEAM-END HEAD'S HALF, off FLANGE_HEAD_D's 17.3 - the bolt that goes into a beam's corner bores, which his rule 2026-10-08 keeps at the old style. ⚠ THE FRONT STRIP'S BOLT IS A DIFFERENT PART at 13.8, so its half is 6.9: use FLANGE_STRIP_D for anything on that joint. This symbol briefly read 6.9 on 2026-10-08 when the strip bolt was wrongly written into FLANGE_HEAD_D, which would have relaxed every edge distance in the repo on the strength of a bolt that is not in those joints. |
| **FLANGE_DRIVE** | 0 mm | part |  | NOT A LENGTH - a fact parked where the other fastener facts live, because it changes how a joint is assembled. Both the M8 and M5 flange fasteners are FLANGED BUTTON HEADS DRIVEN BY A HEX SOCKET in the centre of the dome, settled 2026-10-03. Two consequences. (1) They need AXIAL access for a hex key and cannot be driven by a spanner, so anywhere a bolt sits in a narrow slot the key reaches it where a wrench never would - the front strip's rows, 45 between the bearing block rows, are the case in point. (2) The whole head is FLANGE_HEAD_H or FLANGE_M5_H proud and no more; nothing sits above the dome. |
| **RAIL_BOLT_HOLE_D** | 6 mm | vendor |  | 6, the rail's through-hole - Vevor HGH block page, column d. 🔴 THE 0.5 OF RADIAL FLOAT ON AN M5 IS NOT SLOP, IT IS THE MECHANISM. It is what lets a bolt tilt to catch a T-nut thread that is not perfectly aligned, and what lets the rail be nudged into line. He found an M6 would enter but not wiggle, and concluded the bolts would have to be pre-threaded into their T-nuts and slid in one at a time - 51 assemblies by hand. That difficulty WAS the symptom: a mounting hole with no clearance is the wrong bolt, not a hard job. |
| **BOLT_RAIL** | 16 mm | vendor |  | M5 x 16 for every rail mounting bolt - Vevor HGH block page. Socket head 8.5 across, which seats in the 9.5 counterbore with 0.5 to spare where an M6's 10.0 will not go in at all. |
| **RAIL_CBORE_D** | 9.5 mm | vendor |  | 9.5, the counterbore along an HGR20 rail - Vevor HGH block page, column D, and he confirms it on the part. Was carried as 10. 🔴 IT IS WHAT SETTLED THE M5-versus-M6 ARGUMENT: the manual contradicts itself, the block page giving M5 x 16 with D 9.5 / h 8.5 / d 6 and the rail page giving S = M6 x 1P. An M6 SOCKET HEAD IS 10.0 ACROSS AND CANNOT SIT IN A 9.5 COUNTERBORE - he tried it. The block page is right, the rail page is an error, and Sheet 3a's fourteen M5 holes stand as drawn. |
| **RAIL_CBORE_DEPTH** | 8.5 mm | vendor |  | 8.5, the counterbore depth - Vevor HGH block page, column h, confirmed on the part. Was carried as 10, which also made the rail look like half its 17.5 height. It is one term in how far a hex driver has to reach to a rail bolt through the Z plate and spacer. |
| **RAIL_CBORE_FIRST** | 20 mm | part |  | First counterbore from either end of a rail - the pattern is symmetric, 20 in from both ends with RAIL_CBORE_PITCH between. |
| **RAIL_CBORE_PITCH** | 60 mm | part |  | Counterbore pitch along the rail. |
| **RAIL_CBORE_N_BEAM** | 17 mm | derived | ((BEAM_LEN - (2 * RAIL_CBORE_FIRST)) / RAIL_CBORE_PITCH) + 1 | 17 on a 1000 rail. | **RAIL_CBORE_N_Z** | 7 mm | derived | ((Z_RAIL_L - (2 * RAIL_CBORE_FIRST)) / RAIL_CBORE_PITCH) + 1 | 7 on the 400 Z rail. Also exact, on the same pattern. |

| **BLOCK_OVERHANG_CLEAR** | 6 mm | measured |  | Clear height under the HGH20 block, above the surface the rail sits on. His, 2026-10-03, stated as AT MOST 6 - so it is an upper bound, and anything designed against it should leave room. 🔴 WAS 4.5 from the 2026-09-29 bench table. The 6 is the better number because IT PREDICTS BOTH OF HIS MEASURED OUTCOMES, where 4.5 only predicted one: a 4 mm strip stacks to 5 and fits, a 1/4in strip stacks to 7.35 and does not. At 4.5 the 4 mm case came out marginal on paper while fitting in practice, which was the tell that the clearance figure was wrong rather than the fit. IT IS THE CEILING ON ANYTHING THAT REACHES UNDER THE BLOCK. |

None of that applies now; nothing goes under the block. See STRIP_STACK, which existed to bound it. |

The strip is NOT T_BACK_JOIN_PLATE - they shared 6.35 once and are different parts with different constraints; the back plate is sized for stiffness, the strip by what clears a block overhang. See gantry-beam-joint.md for the stiffness given up. |
| **TSLOT_LIP_T** | 2.3 mm | measured |  | Thickness of the T-slot lip on the 30-6060 - the shoulder a slide-in T-nut bears against, so it is also HOW DEEP the nut's back face starts. His calipers, 2026-10-04. The 8020 section drawing calls the lip 4.20, which is a DIFFERENT dimension (the lip's reach inward, not its thickness) and must not be substituted here. This is one of the two numbers that decide bolt length; nothing in the repo had it before. |
| **TSLOT_DEPTH** | 9.5 mm | measured |  | Beam face to T-slot FLOOR on the 30-6060. His calipers, 2026-10-04. The other half of the bolt-length calculation, and the figure the published section does not give: the drawing dimensions the slot's mouth (8.14) and channel width (16.51) but never its depth, which is why bolt lengths could not be computed before this was taken. |
| **TNUT_BODY_T** | 6 mm | measured |  | 8020 13025 T-nut body thickness where the thread runs - 6, his calipers 2026-10-04, confirming the published F = 6.00. THIS IS THE CEILING ON THREAD ENGAGEMENT for every bolt-on plate on every beam: the bolt cannot engage more than 6 mm no matter how long it is, so engagement is set by the nut and not by the bolt. The nut's total height is 7.80 including its 1.80 boss, and that boss is not threaded usefully - do not compute engagement off 7.80. |
| **TNUT_BACK_FACE** | 8.3 mm | derived | TSLOT_LIP_T + TNUT_BODY_T | Where the T-nut's back face sits below the beam face: 8.3. The boss (1.80) is SHORTER than the lip (2.3), so the nut's shoulders bear on the lip underside and the boss top sits 0.5 recessed from the face - which means the lip thickness, not the boss, is what sets this depth. |
| **TNUT_BACK_CLEAR** | 1.2 mm | derived | TSLOT_DEPTH - TNUT_BACK_FACE | Air behind the T-nut, between its back face and the slot floor: 1.2. THIS IS THE PROTRUSION BUDGET - how far a bolt tip may stand proud of the nut before it bottoms on the slot floor. A bolt that bottoms reads as a tight bolt that never pulls the plate down, which is the failure this symbol exists to prevent. |
| **BOLT_REACH_MAX** | 7.2 mm | derived | TNUT_BODY_T + TNUT_BACK_CLEAR | 7.2 - the most a bolt may reach past the back face of any plate bolted to a beam. Bolt length minus plate thickness must not exceed this. It is what rules M8 x 12 OUT on the 4 mm front strip (reach 8.0) while leaving it correct on the 6.35 back plate (reach 5.65). |

## Not confirmed on the real part

🔴 **OPEN** values are placeholders and **must not be cut to.** ⚠️ **nominal** values are
catalogue figures not yet checked against the part - the class that produced three wrong
numbers in one session on 2026-10-02.

- **T_SOLE_BRACKET** (nominal) = 6.35 mm - feeds 1: Y_NUT_BOLT_ENGAGE
- **FIN_KERF** (nominal) = 2 mm - nothing depends on it
- **SPACER_T** (OPEN) = 15.2 mm - feeds 3: GANTRY_ARM, SPINDLE_OFFSET, Z_BOLT_ENGAGE
- **T_Z_PLATE** (nominal) = 12.7 mm - feeds 4: GANTRY_ARM, SPINDLE_OFFSET, Z_CBORE_DEPTH, Z_NUT_CBORE_DEPTH
- **T_X_CARRIAGE_PLATE** (nominal) = 12.7 mm - feeds 1: GANTRY_ARM
- **SHELF_BAR_W** (nominal) = 25.4 mm - feeds 1: SHELF_SHIM_W
